subject: english-literature
title: Archetypes and Adaptation
welcome_lead: Frye's archetypal patterns and Genette's hypertextuality help map how stories recur across forms and centuries.
meta_desc: English Literature: archetypal patterns, Frye, and the theory of literary adaptation.
final_note: Stories don't end — they migrate and transform.

concepts.def: A recurring symbol, character or pattern across literature (Frye, Jung).
Northrop Frye's approach grouping literature into seasonal mythoi: comedy, romance, tragedy, irony.
Transposing a text into a new medium or genre.
A text derived from a prior text (hypotext) through transformation or imitation.
Genette's term for serious transformation, e.g. Joyce's Ulysses from the Odyssey.
Archetypal journey involving departure, trial and return.

walkthroughs.body_html: Frye links genres to seasons: comedy = spring, romance = summer, tragedy = autumn, irony/satire = winter. Mapping a text to a mythos clarifies its emotional arc.
A film adaptation is also a reading. Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet recasts Verona as a contemporary city, foregrounding youth alienation.
Transposition takes a hypotext seriously into a new key. Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea transposes Jane Eyre's Bertha into a postcolonial protagonist.
